checks.claim: Chip-grade silicon must be at least about nine nines (99.9999999 percent) pure, roughly one foreign atom per billion, with top grades even purer.
checks.why: 9N is the commonly quoted figure and the arithmetic holds, but sources differ on the exact requirement (some say 99.99999 percent or higher, others eleven nines), so hedged wording is safer.

sources.title: Process for the production of medium and high purity silicon from metallurgical grade silicon

checks.claim: Silicon is made by heating quartz with carbon in an electric arc furnace at up to about 2,000 °C (industry ranges run from roughly 1,500 or 1,300 °C up to 2,000 °C).
checks.why: The process is right, but the 1,900 to 2,000 °C figure comes from a small recycling furnace study, not a general industrial figure. Industrial sources give 1,500 to 2,000 °C or 1,300 to 2,000 °C. This step also yields only metallurgical-grade silicon, which needs much more purification.
